related_questions.question: Is there a virus going around that causes a rash?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, several viruses can cause rashes. These rashes are often called viral exanthems. Some common viruses known to cause rashes include chickenpox (varicella-zoster virus), measles (morbillivirus), rubella (rubella virus), and hand, foot, and mouth disease (coxsackievirus). Other viruses like parvovirus B19 (Fifth disease) and human herpesvirus 6 (Roseola) can also cause rashes.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, several viruses can cause rashes

list.snippet: Chickenpox (varicella-zoster virus): Causes a blister-like rash.
Measles (morbillivirus): Causes a red, blotchy rash.
Rubella (rubella virus): Causes a pink or red rash.
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (coxsackievirus): Causes sores in the mouth and a rash on the hands and feet.
Fifth disease (parvovirus B19): Causes a "slapped cheek" rash.
Roseola (human herpesvirus 6): Causes a high fever followed by a rash.

text_blocks.snippet: Rashes from viral infections can vary in appearance, causing bumps, spots, or changes in skin color. They may also be itchy or painful.

related_questions.question: What can cause sudden rashes all over the body?

text_blocks.snippet: Sudden rashes all over the body can be caused by a variety of factors, including allergic reactions, infections, and autoimmune conditions. Allergic reactions, such as those to medications or food, can trigger hives, which are itchy, red or skin-colored bumps that appear suddenly. Infections like measles, mononucleosis, and scarlet fever can also cause widespread rashes. Additionally, certain autoimmune diseases, like lupus, can manifest with skin rashes.
snippet_highlighted_words: allergic reactions, infections, and autoimmune conditions

list.title: Hives (Urticaria):
list.snippet: These are raised, red or skin-colored bumps that can appear suddenly and may be itchy or painful. They can be triggered by various allergens, including foods, medications, insect bites, or even extreme temperatures.

list.title: Drug Reactions:
list.snippet: Some medications can cause skin rashes as a side effect, which can range from mild to severe.

list.title: Contact Dermatitis:
list.snippet: This occurs when the skin comes into direct contact with an irritant or allergen, such as poison ivy, certain cosmetics, or soaps.
Viral Infections: Measles, chickenpox, and mononucleosis are examples of viral infections that can cause widespread rashes.
Bacterial Infections: Scarlet fever, caused by bacteria, can also lead to a rash.
Fungal Infections: While fungal infections often cause localized rashes, some can spread and cause more generalized symptoms.

list.title: Lupus:
list.snippet: This autoimmune disease can cause a variety of skin rashes, including the characteristic butterfly rash on the face.

list.title: Psoriasis:
list.snippet: Psoriasis can cause red, scaly patches on the skin, which may or may not be itchy.

list.title: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis):
list.snippet: This chronic condition can cause red, itchy, and scaly rashes, especially in areas where skin folds.
Heat Rash: Occurs when sweat ducts are blocked, trapping sweat under the skin, causing small, itchy bumps.
Medications: Certain medications can cause rashes as a side effect, especially those that cause photosensitivity (increased sensitivity to sunlight).
Stress: Stress can exacerbate existing skin conditions or even trigger new rashes.

text_blocks.snippet: If you experience a sudden rash accompanied by difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness, or a fever, seek immediate medical attention, according to Healthdirect. It is also recommended to consult a doctor if the rash is painful, blistering, or if you have any concerns about its appearance or severity.
